narrative:
During a heavy rainstorm, two aluminium composite panels (component of the external cladding material for the 
Office building) dislodged and dropped. The two (2) panels, each weighing 9.8kgs and measuring 1.11x1.49ms, 
dropped from about a height of 22.35 meters. The fallen panels were found Infront of the South Wing Power room, 
and the affected area was promptly cordoned off to prevent further hazards. Additionally, multiple panels were 
observed hanging loosely, posing a potential safety risk to occupants and visitors.
what_went_wrong:
1. Aluminium composite panels not airtight. - Previous investigations revealed that no consideration was given 
to the potential for panels falling during design and installation. Furthermore, subsequent structural integrity 
assessments did not clearly establish the mode of failure and effective mitigation measures to prevent recurrence.
Additionally, in cases where potentially falling aluminium composite panels have been reported, remedial actions to 
remove and reinstall such panels are not promptly executed, despite the high potential impact of a dropped panel.
2. Corrective action process not effectively implemented. - There has been recurring near misses involving dropped 
Aluminium Composite Panels in 2016, 2017, 2018, and 2024. However, corrective actions, such as implementing 
monthly and quarterly drop inspections, have not been sustained.
Furthermore, planned preventive maintenance and other assurance activities that were instituted have not been 
consistently followed and remain areas requiring improvement. For instance, the annual integrity assessment for 
2023 and 2024 were not conducted as planned.
corrective_actions:
1. Conduct an integrity inspection and assessment of the external of the entire building to identify any areas of loose 
cladding and fix them immediately to prevent any potential recurrence of the incident in the short term.
2. Re-institute the conduct of the annual inspection programme of the entire exterior of the building's facade to 
identify any areas of loose cladding and fix them immediately to prevent any potential dropped objects.

• Unsafe practice had become normalised due to prior similar lifts performed without incident.

• Never route loads through hatches/openings without engineered lifting arrangements.
• Maintain line of sight or use a designated trained signalman with agreed communication protocol.

• Verify competency and certification of riggers and lifting personnel.

industry: Oil and Gas Exploration and Production
cause: Falls from height
narrative:
On an offshore drilling rig, on 1 September 2025, personnel and marine crew were installing handrails on top of a 
unit on the main deck. Handrail sections (60–90 kg) were lifted by deck crane to the top of the unit, where an operator 
worked at height to receive and install them, using fall-arrest equipment. The operator initially attached his lanyard 
to the stairs, then to handrail, and later to another section to reach the final corner section. To fit the last section, he 
had to lift and adjust some of the handrail. The locking pins were weakly retained and the chain/carabiner secondary 
securing arrangement did not prevent them from sliding out. The section of the handrail tilted and fell, pulling the 
operator with it. He fell approximately 4.3 m to deck, landing partly on the fallen handrail. The incident resulted in an 
LTI and a dropped object with calculated energy of 2733 J, with assessed potential for a single fatality.
what_went_wrong:
The units were not designed to support safe work at height: the only structurally adequate anchoring points (lifting 
eyes) were located below top deck level and were occupied by lifting bridles during installation, leaving no suitable 
anchor points available. The operator therefore clipped his fall-arrest lanyard to a handrail section that was only 
temporarily secured by a pin, chain, and carabiner. The handrail securing design was inherently weak; on the short 
side of the container, the locking pin had only ~2 mm mechanical engagement and could easily slide out, and the 
chain/carabiner arrangement offered a false sense of security. The installation and commissioning procedure 
mentioned work at height and scaffolding, but did not clearly explain how the handrails should be installed or 
secured, nor the purpose or requirement for scaffold. No scaffold was erected, and the crew changed the intended 
installation sequence, requiring lifting and moving the section used as an anchor. Competence requirements for 
work at height (Norog 113) were not formalised in the competence matrix; several involved personnel lacked formal 
practical WAH training and were unaware of approved anchor point requirements. Project planning and follow-up 
from onshore were insufficient, and the contractor equipment checklist process was not effectively applied.
corrective_actions:
Work at height must never rely on temporary structures (such as partially installed handrails) as anchoring points. 
Units that require routine or installation work at height must be designed with suitable, certified anchor points, or 
work must be carried out from properly designed scaffolding or other engineered access solutions. Competence 
requirements for working at height (incl. practical training and anchor-point assessment) must be explicitly built 
into contractor competence matrices and verified before mobilisation. Installation and commissioning procedures 
for vendor packages must clearly describe safe installation methods, including detailed handrail installation 
sequences, locking mechanisms, and when scaffolding is mandatory. Work permits that bundle many high-
risk activities can obscure critical controls; large scopes should be broken into smaller work procedures where 
necessary to ensure hazards and controls are fully understood. A robust equipment and project-follow-up process 
is needed, including use of the correct contractor equipment checklist and clear assignment of onshore and 
offshore responsibility for installation planning and oversight.

cause: Dropped objects
narrative:
During preparations for installing a 20’’ sealing ring on the platform on 2 July 2025, a technician tested the ring 
for fit before the lift operation. The 7.1 kg ring slipped from the technician’s hands and fell 6.35 meters to the deck 
below, landing approximately two meters from a mechanic who was grinding at deck level. The ring then bounced 
and struck the mechanic on the arm. The mechanic received a first-aid level impact with no observable injury. The 
event had a severe potential for fatality due to the weight and fall height. The ring had been brought into the elevated 
work area earlier than planned, the area was insufficiently barricaded, and the test occurred without notification to 
the crew below. Multiple procedural, communication and barrier-management weaknesses contributed.
what_went_wrong:

the crew below. The ring slipped due to inadequate handling conditions (gloves, oily surface). The work area had 
been split into two phases, but equipment was still placed in the elevated area during phase one, creating exposure 
before barriers were in place. Barricading was too small, based on a common but unsafe practice of using minimal 
exclusion zones for “non-loose object” work at height. Communication between team members and between teams 
and was incomplete. The area technician approved only the intent of barricading but did not verify it physically. The 
team lead was cognitively overloaded and new in the role, reducing situational awareness. Stop-work authority was 
not used despite unease among personnel below. The net result was coexistence of workers above and below with 
no effective barrier against dropped objects.

(e.g., safety net) is installed. Equipment must not be brought into elevated areas before controls are in place. Area

not to bring loose items into height work are insufficient; technical and organizational barriers must supplement 
human behaviour. SIMOPS coordination must be strengthened, including explicit identification of all nearby work 
teams and discussion in morning meetings. Communication internally within teams must be improved to ensure 
shared situational awareness. Stop-work authority must be normalised, supported, and used proactively. Project-
wide learning should be shared across platforms to eliminate similar practices elsewhere.

narrative:
On May 20, 2025, a worker was engaged in repositioning a spec blind from the closed to the open position on the 
flare line, in preparation to de-isolate the unit for commissioning activities. During this activity, the worker was 
exposed to a gas/energy release from the down steam side of the isolated gate valve at the open flange pair. Worker 
required rescue from heights and was provided onsite first aid; worker was transported to a local hospital for 
further medical assessment where it was determined worker sustained bruised ribs and a concussion. Worker was 
released from hospital the same day.
what_went_wrong:
The 10” gate valve used as a single isolation was not fully closed because the chain operator seized due to physical 
interference, giving a false indication that the valve was seated. Pressure verification showed 0 kPag, but this was 
ambiguous because the flare system was under slight vacuum, meaning zero pressure did not confirm positive 
isolation. Oxygen entered the flare piping system through the partially open valve while the flare remained lit, 
creating conditions for ignition. When work was performed on the spectacle blind, this led to a deflagration and an 
uncontrolled release of energy that injured the worker.
corrective_actions:
1. Zero pressure does not equal positive isolation - Pressure indication alone is an insufficient barrier for verifying 
isolation in flare systems, especially where vacuum conditions can exist. 
2. Single isolation is not a robust barrier for breaking containment - Single isolation provides little tolerance for 
hidden failures and should not be relied upon where severe energy release is credible. 
3. Equipment condition and work environment directly shape human decision-making - People act on the cues the 
system gives them; degraded equipment and obstructed layouts can actively mislead competent workers. 
4. Permits and risk classification must reflect real hazard potential - Administrative controls lose credibility when 
they do not reflect the true severity of the hazard.

narrative:
On 04 September 2025, an uncontrolled release of approximately 1,064 kg of hydrocarbon and inert gas mixture 
occurred from the cargo tank vent lines on an FPSO, resulting in Emergency Shutdown activation. The release was

No formal agreement with supplier on timelines for firmware fixes or release notes during commissioning.
A software backup was performed during cold venting activities without prior communication between the ICSS FSR 
and the operations team. Additionally, the ICSS FSR did not verify the card restart configuration before generating 
and uploading the backup. The controller’s configuration module was set to return to its “last saved” value upon 
restart when redundancy was not available.
Daily check for monitoring overall controller status was not established at this stage (Commissioning + Operation).
CROs not focus on system alarms at this stage (Commissioning + Operation).
Onboard team relied on verbal risk assessment. MOC “Deviation” exists, but triggers unclear for abnormal 
conditions.

• Develop and formalize a clear process that defines timelines and responsibilities for execution of anomalies 
and/or safety alerts.
• Conduct a comprehensive review of all controller module parameter configurations to confirm the safest restart 
settings are applied.
• Establish procedure to manage software changes during commissioning.
• For future projects, in alignment with the established process philosophy and specifically for systems that may 
result in unintended hydrocarbon releases to the atmosphere, it is essential to verify and define the software 
configurations during the engineering phase. These settings should ensure that actuated valves assume the 
safest possible position during restart conditions.
• Develop and implement a daily controller status verification checklist for the DCS Technician detailing specific 
items to check, timing, and completion steps.

industry: Oil and Gas Production and Operations
narrative:
An incident occurred during the transfer of an amine solution from a truck to a storage tank. The transfer 
was performed using a corrugated flexible hose connected to the truck with a threaded coupling and to the 
tank with a metal clamp. The end of the transfer was verified by observing hose vibrations generated during 
nitrogen displacement operations. After completing the transfer, one operator closed the nitrogen valve used for 
pressurization toward the truck and visually confirmed closure of the amine discharge valve on the truck. The 
second operator entered the containment area to close the tank valves. After closing the needle valve located near 
the tank, while attempting to close the ball valve, the hose suddenly detached from the nozzle, causing an amine 
splash that hit the operator’s face through a gap between the visor and the chin. While attempting to wash at the 
eyewash station, the operator rubbed his face and eyes with contaminated hands, worsening the injury. He was 
immediately assisted by a colleague, taken to the infirmary, and then transported to the emergency room.
what_went_wrong:
Design: the absence of a non-return valve in the tank isolation circuit was identified, although it was included in the 
reference P&ID. The NRV was designed to be installed between the two tank isolation valves. Its presence would 
have prevented the incident by avoiding amine backflow into the final section of the pipeline, caused by the tank 
head, during the operator’s movement from the truck to the tank to perform valve closure and tank isolation.
Management of Change: A MoC was underway to replace the current metal clamp fastening system used to connect 
the corrugated hose to the storage tank connections with safer fittings connections. The MoC process had started 
two years earlier. Engineering activities had been completed, and implementation had been finalized for some tanks 
but not yet for the tank involved in the incident.
Operational Procedure Misalignment: The existing loading procedure had been issued for a future plant 
configuration, as it was based on the implementation of the above-mentioned MoC, and therefore did not reflect the 
current operating conditions of the tank involved. Additionally, although the tank-side valve closing sequence was 
correctly performed by the operator, it did not include a clear and standardized sequence, generating confusion 
among operators due to the absence of a standard valve closure procedure.
Emergency Response Training: Insufficient awareness of decontamination procedures was identified. The eye injury 
occurred when the operator rubbed his eyes with contaminated hands.
corrective_actions:
Ensure technical/operational integrity: Verify that all design specifications are met during construction and 
installation. Address safety operational improvements deviations promptly through a completed MoC process and 
always ensure dedicated risk assessment which identifies possible mitigation measures to be implemented.
Keep procedures current: Operating procedures must reflect actual plant conditions, with clear roles, 
responsibilities, and standardized sequences
Strengthen emergency preparedness: Conduct regular training and drills for chemical exposure scenarios, 
including loading/unloading operations, to reinforce response protocols.

narrative:
During a routine condensate tanker loading operation at Loading Bay, an overfill occurred resulting in an 
estimated loss of 1040 kg of condensate. The event resulted from the failure of the High-High level switch, which 
did not initiate the automatic system shutdown as designed. The abnormal condition was identified through

emergency shutdown push button, thereby halting loading operations.

what_went_wrong:
1. Failure of Primary Level Control Barrier- high-high level switch failed to operate and did not initiate the automatic 
closure of the associated loading valves (XV and SDV).
2. Design Flaws in Timer-Based Overfill Protection - The tertiary overfill protection relied on a preset loading timer 
based on a fixed batch concept, which did not account for varying tanker sizes or flow rates.
3. Redundant Barrier Not Maintained in Practice - A local high-level switch, previously identified as a safety barrier 
in earlier designs and referenced in the Control and Operating Philosophy, was retained physically but removed as a 
functional barrier during the re-HAZOP.
4. Procedural and Human Factors Weaknesses - Although pre-loading checks are required, they did not adequately 
account for the degraded condition of key safeguards. 
The dependency on a single barrier and the lack of operator awareness about available fallback systems further 
compounded the risk.
corrective_actions:
1. Remove the logic for the end of sequence timer protection and remove its reference from the Control and 
Philosophy procedure. 
2. Carry out an ergonomic design assessment of the Hatch Cover assembly.
3. Incorporate the local high-level Alarm as the secondary barrier.
4. Conduct a comprehensive Safety Critical Task Analysis’s (SCTA) of the NGL road tanker loading operation. 
5. Develop detailed Standard Operating Procedures (SOP) for the NGL/LPG and tanker loading process.
6. Deliver a training program to all affected stakeholders.

corrective_actions:
Valve interventions on large-diameter systems are high-risk activities and require strict control of stored energy 
(pressure, mechanical, gravitational).
Full isolation, depressurization, verification of zero energy, and mechanical securing of components must be 
completed before any work begins.
Exclusion zones and line-of-fire controls are mandatory when working with heavy or potentially mobile metallic 
components.
Trainees must not be exposed to critical tasks without direct supervision, clear role definition, and confirmation of 
competency.
Permit to Work (PTW), Job Safety Analysis (JSA), and LOTO procedures must explicitly address:
• Component movement or ejection.
• Required restraints and tooling.
• Safe positioning of personnel.
Contractor safety management must ensure alignment with site standards, including training, supervision, and 
enforcement of stop-work authority.

assumptions; verification is essential.

measurement tank (TM) area, detecting on site the passage of liquids in the suction valve from TM-1 to the RA-11 
oily register, which caused an increase in levels in the API dam and RA-05 oily registers (separator area), RA-12 
(measuring tank dam) and S/N registers in the area of pumps with hydrocarbon spillage on the ground of these 
areas, immediately an attempt was made to pump with the Internal Combustion Motor Pump 03 (MBCI-03) in a 
discontinuous manner due to the low suction pressure, so the suction valve of the TM-1 was dismantled. managing 
to contain the passage of liquid to the API dam and oily registers with diversion of oil to the TM containment dam 
and later pumping to the vertical tanks through the pump (MBCI-03).
what_went_wrong:
On the day of the event, Tank TM-1 had been dewatered by opening the suction valve towards its base, directing 
water to the API separator via the oily drains. During this operation the water was pumped from the API separator 
to the larger vertical storage tank TV-5. Once the water had been decanted the valve was closed.
Later in the afternoon an operator detected flow in the oily water system and determined that the valve on TM-1 was 
passing. Suspecting debris was lodged beneath the gate, the operator opened the valve to flush the debris and then 
closed it. This and other attempts to fully close the valve were unsuccessful and the operator decided to use a pipe 
wrench to close it. The force broke the lifting nut and there was a significant increase in flow.
Despite the pump running at the API separator and additional pumping of oil to the export system, the site was 
unable to prevent the API separator from being overwhelmed, and oil backflowed up the oil drainage system, 
overtopping covers in several locations to spill onto the concrete hardstanding. A flange was loosened at the suction 
valve on tank TM-1 and the remaining contents of the tank allowed to drain into its containment bund.
About 198bbls of oil was lost from the tank. Most was contained within the drains and the API separator and 
pumped to tank TV-5 or collected by a vacuum truck.

industry: Oil and Gas Production and Operations
narrative:
During a walkthrough on the platform, a worker who was holding the position of Helper C perceived an abnormal 
noise near the fuel gas regulation package, which operates at 74 kg/cm². Upon inspecting the package, he identified 
the presence of gas in a 2” Ø x 600# line located on the mezzanine of the first level.
As he inspected the line more closely, he detected a loss of containment at the threaded connection between the 2” 
Ø x 600# line and the 2” x 600# coupling. He proceeded to tighten the 2” Ø coupling to the 2” Ø pipe, observing that 
the gas emission gradually decreased. Immediately afterward, the threaded coupling detached, leaving his left palm 
exposed to the gas coming out of the pipe.
He immediately informed the Control Room and secured the residual gas system. With support from the first aid 
brigade of the Processing Centre, he was transferred, conscious and walking on his own, from platform to the 
Processing Centre via lateral flight for medical attention.
what_went_wrong:
A loss of containment occurred at a threaded connection on a high-pressure fuel gas line (˜74 kg/cm²).
The worker attempted to tighten a leaking threaded coupling while the line was pressurized, which is unsafe.
Tightening the live connection caused the threaded coupling to fail and detach completely, exposing the worker’s 
hand directly to escaping gas.
Threaded fittings are not robust for high-pressure gas service and are prone to failure due to vibration, wear, 
misalignment, or improper makeup.
Immediate isolation and depressurization were not performed before intervention, increasing the risk of injury and 
escalation.
corrective_actions:
Never tighten or repair a leaking pressurized gas connection. Any gas leak must trigger stop work, evacuation, 
notification to the Control Room, isolation, and depressurization.
Threaded connections should be avoided in high-pressure fuel gas systems; welded or flanged joints are safer and 
more reliable.

coating failure, or mechanical damage near the field joint area.

Field joints are critical integrity points and require enhanced inspection, monitoring, and protection, especially 
during subsea or underwater activities.

performed before and during such work.

must be clearly defined and applied.

industry: Oil and Gas Production and Operations
narrative:
On March 7th, 2025, the platform experienced a major process safety incident when the hinge pin of the dome 
on a Cargo Tank starboard catastrophically failed. The rupture of the hinge pin resulted in the complete loss of 
mechanical restraint of the dome, causing the dome cover to fully open and exposing the entire tank opening to 
atmosphere. This structural failure led to the uncontrolled release of a flammable gas mixture directly onto the deck.
The plant’s gas detection system was activated, initiating an emergency shutdown (ESD). Personnel were mustered 
in the accommodation module; however, a continuous flammable gas cloud was extending laterally across the full 
width of the platform, spanning from one side to the other. As a result, access to the muster location necessarily 
required personnel to pass through the flammable gas cloud.
The tanks were depressurized both through the fully open dome, which was already providing an unrestricted 
release path, and by remotely opening the vent stacks. Despite these depressurization measures, the uncontrolled 
release continued for nearly one hour, until the tanks were fully vented and pressure equalized with the atmosphere.
Fortunately, there were no injuries, fires, explosions, or environmental impacts. Nevertheless, production was 
halted, and personnel were exposed to significant risk due to the prolonged presence of a flammable atmosphere 
across the installation.
what_went_wrong:
The root cause investigation identified that the main threat was progressive corrosion on the dome’s hinge pin, 
caused by an inadequate weld that was smaller than specified in the original design. Weaknesses in the preventive 
safety barriers allowed this defect to persist: the inspection plan did not require detailed checks on the dome pin, 
and a maintenance anomaly had been incorrectly reported in the system (as a generic defect note instead of a 
specific inspection note, and linked to a general location instead of the dome pin). These failures in inspection and 
anomaly management meant the integrity problem was neither prioritized nor properly addressed, allowing the 
degradation to continue unnoticed until catastrophic failure.
corrective_actions:
The incident highlighted the need for robust inspection and maintenance protocols focused on critical structural 
joints of tank covers. Inspections must be properly planned and rigorously executed to verify weld quality, 
dimensional compliance, and integrity at hinge assemblies, pivot points, and attachment areas. Maintenance 
reporting processes should require precise classification and direct linkage of each finding to the exact component 
affected, avoiding generic location references. Information management systems must include all relevant 
structural elements to prevent misregistration or omission of critical observations.
Design and procurement standards should mandate verification of structural joints and weld integrity at 
commissioning and throughout the operational lifecycle, incorporating these checks into routine field inspections.

narrative:
A severe industrial accident occurred on an offshore production platform during gas import operations. At the 
time, the platform was in the process of decommissioning, with most production systems already shut down and 
being readied for dismantling; only the gas import line remained operational to supply the power generator. On 
the morning of the incident, this last active pipeline ruptured after years of progressive corrosion, which developed 
specifically on its upper surface - an area exposed to salty water dripping through an unsealed opening between 
decks directly above. Because the line was installed in an elevated position, the most recent inspections did not fully 
address the upper side, allowing a localized, severe corrosion spot on the top of the pipe to go undetected. When the 
rupture finally occurred, a large volume of flammable gas was released and quickly ignited, resulting in a powerful 
jet fire and vapor cloud explosion. Multiple workers were injured, rescue efforts were hampered by equipment 
failures and communication problems, and the event resulted in significant material damage and evacuation of the 
platform.

what_went_wrong:
Several systemic and technical failures contributed to the accident. Key inspections and planned maintenance 
activities, including the painting and full-circumference inspection of the pipeline, were not prioritized or effectively 
carried out, partly due to resource constraints and difficulties with access. Procedures for sealing penetrations 
between decks, established to prevent transfer of water and other substances, were not thoroughly implemented, 
enabling persistent water leaks onto the pipeline. The corrosion process was not anticipated nor reassessed, 
despite past records of similar damage in other areas. In addition, operational management did not ensure that 
the maximum safe pressure for pipeline operation matched actual technical recommendations. Critical barriers 
such as the automatic firewater system and fire detection did not act fully as designed, prolonging firefighting and 
evacuation efforts. Emergency communication was hampered both by structural damage and lack of robust back-
up systems.
corrective_actions:
The accident highlighted the critical importance of robust asset integrity management, disciplined risk assessment 
processes, clearly defined operational limits, and reliable emergency and communication systems in complex 
offshore environments. These elements are particularly vital during transitional phases such as decommissioning, 
when operational priorities shift and legacy assets may operate under reduced monitoring. The event reinforced the 
need for structured preventive maintenance, integrated risk-based decision-making, strengthened organizational 
learning, and resilient emergency preparedness. It also emphasized that procedures, responsibilities, and any 
deferral or cancellation of maintenance must be transparent, technically justified, and consistently documented 
across all management levels.
Based on these learnings, the key recommendations are:
• Enforce comprehensive inspection regimes, especially in hard-to-access areas, ensuring systemic asset 
monitoring independent of individual discretion.
• Strengthen governance for prioritization and timely closure of maintenance actions, avoiding backlog 
accumulation.
• Implement formal controls for sealing and segregation between platform areas, integrating these into design 
and modification reviews.
• Align operational risk thresholds, such as pressure limits, with updated technical assessments through 
structured cross-functional reviews.
• Institutionalize periodic reviews of material selection and asset specifications, embedding fire and chemical 
resistance criteria into procurement standards.
• Maintain strict oversight of automatic detection and protection systems, including testing, availability 
monitoring, and performance documentation.
• Establish redundant, independent emergency communication channels and routinely verify their resilience.
• Reinforce policies for fire-resistant PPE, including third-party certification and supplier compliance updates.
• Regularly exercise emergency response plans through scenario-based simulations, including degraded 
communication and multi-asset events.
• Audit inspection, documentation, and information management systems to ensure accuracy, clear accountability, 
and organizational learning.

temporary impairments.

The event originated from a failure in the flexible pipeline at a connector that had been assembled without specific 
mounting controls. The failure mechanism involved stress corrosion cracking induced by CO2, made possible or 
accelerated due to several compounding factors: inadequate risk differentiation for connectors assembled without 
precise tools, use of a less conservative methodology for determining component lifespan, and high mechanical 
stress associated with field conditions. Critically, a key automatic safety shutdown system had been intentionally 
disabled for operational reasons and was not reactivated—a gap in procedural compliance and communication, 
delaying the response and increasing the volume released.
corrective_actions:
The main lessons centre on the need for robust integrity management systems, effective barrier monitoring, clear 
operational interfaces between different teams, and consistent risk evaluation practices. The event underscored 
that comprehensive controls, adherence to defined procedures, and thorough risk communication are essential for 
preventing escalation, even in the presence of complex technical threats.
Key recommendations and management learnings:
• Adopt stricter controls regarding the differentiated risk of assembling connectors without precision mounting 
tools, integrating this consideration into the overall integrity management system.
• Ensure that risk acceptance criteria for lifetime management are appropriately conservative, especially 
when dealing with known threat mechanisms—periodically revalidate methodologies and revisit underlying 
assumptions.
• Implement and enforce clear procedures for disabling and reactivating safety barriers, particularly those 
associated with interdependent operational areas; ensure all inactivations have documented risk assessment 
and multidisciplinary review.
• Reinforce monitoring routines for all inhibited safety systems, including automated notifications and prompt 
follow-up to minimize periods of exposure.
• Strengthen operational interface and communication protocols between onshore support, oversight, and field 
personnel to guarantee mutual awareness and immediate response capability when critical safety systems are 
inhibited or restored.

validating that replacements or upgrades address all known failure modes.

to recirculation or discharge operations, preventing unintentional product releases.

industry: Oil and Gas Production and Operations
narrative:
A significant release of flammable gas occurred in a subsea production system when the small-diameter pipe 
responsible for chemical injection instrumentation failed completely. The incident went initially unnoticed by 
automatic safety systems. The escape of gas was eventually discovered during scheduled activities using remotely 
operated equipment for another purpose. The event resulted in a discharge of a large volume of gas into the sea; no 
injuries or direct material impact were reported.
what_went_wrong:
The root cause of the incident was mechanical fatigue of the chemical injection tubing, caused by vibration 
induced by gas flow over time. At the design stage, there were no requirements or practices for assessing the risk 
of vibration on such instrumentation lines attached to the pressure containment body. As a result, the primary 
containment barrier for the chemical injection line failed due to degradation from vibration in a so-called “dead leg” 
configuration. Contributing to the incident, the automated safety and shutdown systems did not detect the event: the 
variation in operational pressure was too small to trigger shutoff actions. The shutdown was performed manually 
after detection.
corrective_actions:
This incident demonstrates the importance of systematically managing vibration risks in all pressurized 
instrumented lines, including those not traditionally subject to such analysis. It highlights the necessity to embed 
vibration assessment requirements in the technical specifications and project phases for new and existing 
installations. Strengthening the design and verification process helps to ensure the integrity of barriers and timely 
detection of degradation mechanisms that automated process systems may not catch.
Key recommendations derived from the case include:
• Review and update technical requirements for new projects so that analysis for vibration effects, including 
acoustic and flow-induced vibration, is explicitly required for all instrumented lines attached to the main process 
body.
• For systems currently under construction, ensure that vibration studies are extended to cover these instrument 
tubing lines before commissioning.
• For systems already in operation, develop engineering improvements and plan the implementation to ensure 
that all elements subject to comparable service conditions are covered for integrity over their life cycle.
• Calibrate and implement analytical tools to be capable of estimating the time to failure due to vibration fatigue in 
small-bore instrument lines.
• Based on these studies, create specific action plans for each affected facility, including possible reduction of 
operating parameters, scheduled removals, or engineering retrofits needed to guarantee long-term reliability.

flammable gas mixture occurred. The release happened as the maintenance crew attempted to perform a sequence

execution, with insufficient focus on detailed planning and inspection prior to the task. Administrative safeguards 
failed, particularly in terms of controlling the tools used and ensuring workers possessed the specific technical 
competence demanded by both the process and normative standards. While layered protections such as emergency 
shutdown and gas detection responded effectively to limit escalation, preventive measures did not.
corrective_actions:
This event underscored that high-criticality tasks like hot bolting demand strict compliance with technical 
standards, practical procedures that are clearly defined and executable, and that relying solely on administrative 
controls is inadequate. The organization must ensure that risk assessments and planning encompass real 
working conditions and that exposure to hazardous situations is controlled by robust physical, engineering, and 
organizational safeguards rather than individual choices.

Revise technical standards for hot bolting to ensure that all engineering risk assessment items are addressed 
during planning, documented and implemented in execution.
Update procedures so they fully comply with all normative requirements, and reinforce the need for strict adherence 
in execution—as deviations may lead to uncontrolled loss of containment.
Adapt the permit to work system to explicitly prohibit unsuitable tools (such as hammers) for hot bolting, 
incorporating regulatory restrictions.

ensure only appropriately trained personnel are assigned to such critical tasks.

detached, leading to the release of flammable gas. The gas leak was detected by multiple gas sensors, prompting

lacked clear instructions for properly evaluating small-diameter valves, which made the detection of advanced

double isolation mechanism, allowing gas to pass through manual valves and consequently increasing the volume 
released.

accessories, especially small-diameter valves and those involving dissimilar materials. It reinforced the need for 
robust procedures, quality control, and adherence to engineering best practices across similar operations.

• Revise technical specifications and procedures to ensure they address risks associated with dissimilar 
materials.
• Conduct technical workshops for inspection teams on failure mechanisms in small-diameter valves (mainly 
dissimilar materials).
• Establish integrity evaluations for valves in similar operational conditions and replace those showing signs of 
galvanic corrosion.
• Prohibit the use of dissimilar materials in valves for new projects.

a water bath to prove leak tight. The valve was stroked during this test. The valve is now back in service.
